lessons.title: Pasture species and how grass grows
lessons.html:
Pasture as the cheapest feed

Well-managed pasture is usually the lowest-cost feed per kilogram of dry matter on a dairy. Pasture-based systems in the Eastern Cape, southern Cape and KZN Midlands depend on growing and using as much quality pasture as possible.

Common dairy pasture species in South Africa

SpeciesTypeNotes
KikuyuPerennial, subtropical (C4)High summer growth, tolerant of grazing; quality drops if allowed to grow long; winter dormant
Perennial ryegrassPerennial, temperate (C3)High quality; needs good rainfall or irrigation; often oversown into kikuyu
Italian and annual ryegrassAnnual or short-livedFast autumn-winter-spring growth; used for winter feed
White and red cloverLegumeFixes nitrogen, raises protein; bloat risk
LucernePerennial legumeDeep-rooted, high protein; mostly cut for hay or grazed carefully inland
Oats and forage sorghumsAnnualUsed to fill seasonal gaps

How grass grows after grazing

After grazing, a grass plant regrows from reserves in its base and from the remaining leaf. Growth follows an S-shaped curve: slow at first when leaf area is small, then rapid, then slowing as the sward closes and older leaves die.

For ryegrass, the leaf stage is a practical guide: grazing at about the two-and-a-half to three-leaf stage per tiller generally balances yield, quality and plant persistence. Grazing too early exhausts reserves; grazing too late wastes leaf to senescence and lowers quality. Kikuyu is managed by keeping it short and leafy to maintain quality.

Residual height

Grazing to an appropriate residual leaves enough leaf for quick regrowth while ensuring cows harvest most of the grown material. Too high a residual wastes feed and lowers future quality; too low a residual slows regrowth and damages plants.

lessons.title: Grazing management and feed budgeting
lessons.html:
Grazing systems

  • Rotational grazing: the pasture is divided into camps or paddocks grazed in sequence, allowing regrowth between grazings.
  • Strip grazing: a fresh strip is allocated each grazing with an electric fence, often with a back fence to protect regrowth.
  • Set stocking: animals stay on one area; less common for high-producing dairy cows.

Rotation length

The rotation length is the number of days between grazings of the same camp. It should follow the growth rate: shorter in fast-growth periods such as spring, longer when growth slows in winter or drought. A fixed rotation regardless of growth leads to either overgrazing or wasted feed.

Measuring pasture cover

Managers estimate kg DM per hectare using a rising plate meter, a pasture ruler, visual assessment calibrated by cutting and weighing, or satellite tools. A regular farm walk, often weekly, records the cover in every camp.

Feed wedge and budgeting

Ranking camps from highest to lowest cover produces a feed wedge. It shows whether there is a surplus (to be cut for silage) or a deficit (needing supplements or a slower rotation).

Example daily budget: 300 cows each needing 16 kg DM from pasture require 4 800 kg DM. If a camp has 2 800 kg DM/ha pre-grazing and the target residual is 1 600 kg DM/ha, the available pasture is 1 200 kg DM/ha. Area needed = 4 800 ÷ 1 200 = 4 ha per day.

Supplementation

When pasture is short, supplement with silage, hay or concentrates. Concentrates also balance pasture's energy shortfall for high yielders. Watch substitution: cows may eat less pasture when given more supplement.

Grazing risks

  • Bloat on clover-rich pasture: introduce gradually, avoid putting hungry cows on lush legumes, use bloat control as advised.
  • Grass tetany (low magnesium) on lush, heavily fertilised grass: provide magnesium as the nutritionist advises.
  • Nitrate poisoning risk on heavily fertilised or stressed forage.
  • Treading damage on wet soils: use stand-off areas.

lessons.title: Soil fertility, irrigation and pasture renewal
lessons.html:
Feeding the soil

High-producing pastures remove large amounts of nutrients. Soil sampling and analysis, usually yearly, guides fertiliser use.

  • pH and lime: many high-rainfall pasture soils are acidic; liming corrects pH and improves nutrient availability.
  • Nitrogen: drives grass growth; applied in split doses according to growth season and response.
  • Phosphorus and potassium: maintained at adequate levels for grass and clover.
  • Effluent: dairy effluent is a nutrient source; account for it in the fertiliser plan and apply it in line with any authorisation under the National Water Act 36 of 1998.

Fertilisers are regulated under Act 36 of 1947. Avoid applying before heavy rain or near watercourses to prevent runoff.

Irrigation

Many SA dairy pastures are irrigated with centre pivots or sprinklers. Schedule irrigation by soil moisture measurements, evapotranspiration data or probes, not by habit. Overirrigation wastes water and electricity and leaches nutrients; underirrigation cuts growth. Water use must comply with the farm's water use entitlements under the National Water Act.

Pasture establishment and renewal

  1. Assess the pasture: species composition, weeds, bare patches, yield.
  2. Choose species and cultivars suited to climate, soil and the feed plan.
  3. Prepare the seedbed or plan oversowing into kikuyu in autumn.
  4. Correct soil fertility before planting.
  5. Sow at the right time, rate and depth.
  6. Manage the first grazings lightly to establish plants.

Weed and pest control

Use integrated control: competitive pasture, correct grazing, mechanical control and registered herbicides or pesticides applied according to the label by trained operators with protective equipment.

Soil conservation

The Conservation of Agricultural Resources Act 43 of 1983 requires land users to protect soil from erosion and to control declared weeds. Avoid overgrazing, maintain ground cover and manage water runoff.

Key points

  • Kikuyu, ryegrass and clover are the main dairy pasture species in SA.
  • Graze ryegrass at about the two-and-a-half to three-leaf stage and to a suitable residual.
  • Match rotation length to growth rate and measure pasture cover regularly.
  • Budget area using available DM per hectare and cow demand.
  • Base fertiliser and irrigation on soil tests and moisture data, within the law.
